Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Three years ago, the sudden flash flood in his coastal neighborhood arrived without warning, turning a familiar street into a churning current of debris and brackish water. Duy had been on a second-floor balcony when the storm surge crested the railing, flooding the space where his family had gathered. He tasted the heavy, metallic silt that splashed over his lips while people rushed past in a panic, some shouting commands, others too afraid to look back. The sheer helplessness of watching the waters rise, combined with the disorienting chaos of strangers acting on instinct, left a permanent imprint on his nervous system. Now, at twenty-two, a UX designer working in a glass-walled studio downtown, Duy knows exactly which moments crack that old wound. When a client presentation slides into a video of a swollen river, or when a sudden gust of wind rattles the building's facade, his shoulders instinctively lock and a sharp, band-like pain tightens across his neck. Within seconds, a wave of physical sickness rolls through him, making his hands tremble as he reaches for water that no longer tastes like anything but stale office air. These trauma-related events do not merely startle him; they pull the flood's narrative forward with such force that the story feels too extreme to be real, as if his own mind is trying to distance him from what actually happened. The physical toll of these moments quickly reshapes how he reads the room. Standing at his desk while the pain radiates, he begins to watch his colleagues' hurried footsteps and hushed phone calls with a cold wariness, convinced that people are not what they seem and that any offer of help is just a polite mask for self-preservation. Over the following months, Duy's routine calcified within the studio's open-plan layout. He stopped attending the firm's casual Friday drinks and began routing all his design feedback through asynchronous tickets, retreating to his ergonomic chair to monitor the room from a safe distance. The memory of the flood never arrived as a clean flashback; instead, it often struck him during a collaborative design sprint, where the terror of the waters would surge through his chest with perfect, image-less intensity. That emotion without image was so consuming that it naturally deepened his suspicion of those around him, reinforcing his belief that he belonged nowhere in a world that had already moved on. Paradoxically, this isolation sharpened his sensitivity to every environmental cue. The more convinced he became that he was set apart from others, the more hyper-aware he grew of minor shifts in office lighting, sudden notifications, or a colleague's offhand comment about the weather. Each new suspicion acted as a magnifying glass for his trauma-related events, which in turn ignited that familiar neck pain and nausea. The intrusion of that unreal taste and emotion without image directly heightened his alertness to these cues, making every minor office shift feel like a fresh threat. Every time the metallic taste of the past surfaced, it convinced him that trusting anyone was a dangerous gamble, and that quiet certainty pushed him further into solitary work hours, ensuring the next trigger would feel even more inevitable. By the time he sat in my intake room, the pattern had quietly rewritten his professional life and fractured his social world. He had turned down two promotions because they required leading collaborative workshops, and he had let his closest friends slowly drift away, unable to explain why a simple dinner invitation suddenly felt like a trap. His desk became a physical buffer against the open floor, a necessary perimeter to keep the studio's ambient stress at bay. What finally drove him to seek help was not just the exhaustion of carrying the weight alone, but the terrifying realization that his own mind had become a closed room with no escape. He hoped to find a way to unclench his shoulders when the sky turned gray, to believe that the people in his office were simply trying to meet deadlines rather than conceal their own fears, and to stop tasting floodwater in a perfectly clean kitchen. Most of all, he was afraid of continuing to watch his life slip through his fingers while waiting for a storm that might never come again, and he desperately wanted to learn how to stand still in the present without bracing for the next collapse.
